**My reasoning as this farmer:**

I've been working this land for 40 years. I know Quzhou's climate — the dry springs, the summer rains that come late, the cold snaps in November. My cabbage-maize-cabbage rotation is the spine of my operation. I run it on 4 mu because it gives me two cabbage harvests plus a maize crop, which my household relies on for grain and I sell the surplus cabbage.

I put 1 mu into chili. The price is good at Quzhou market when the harvest is clean, but it needs attention — I've lost chili to blight before, so I don't cut corners on pesticide applications there. The last mu I cycle: spinach through winter and early spring (my household eats a lot of it and I sell to neighbors), then kidney bean in summer on the same plot. Kidney beans are easy on that soil and I don't need to push nitrogen hard because they fix some themselves.

I use hybrid seeds across the board. I learned 20 years ago that traditional varieties don't justify the saved seed cost — the yield gap is too large. My well gives me reliable irrigation, but I'm not careless — electricity runs money, and I only irrigate at critical stages: seedling establishment, heading for cabbage, tasseling and grain fill for maize, flowering for chili.

I apply fertilizer based on soil needs, not just habit. My phosphorus and potassium go in at base application; nitrogen I split — base and top-dress. I've seen neighbors over-apply nitrogen and end up with loose cabbage heads and lodged maize. I plough after cabbage before maize to break up compaction; rotary tillage for vegetables.
